title: Learn Linux
summary: Use the terminal the way people do every day: look around, move, make, read, search and protect files.

lessons.title: First words with the shell
lessons.story: A terminal is a conversation: you type a command, press Enter, and the computer answers. Let's ask it three simple questions.

steps.task: Ask the computer who you are: type whoami and press Enter.
hints: Open the Terminal (Ctrl+Alt+T), type whoami and press Enter.
steps.explain: whoami prints the user you are logged in as. Everything you do runs as that user.

steps.task: Ask where you are: pwd.
hints: pwd stands for print working directory. Type pwd and press Enter.
steps.explain: You start in your home folder, /home/<you>. The prompt shows it as ~.

steps.task: Look around with ls.
hints: ls lists what is in the current folder. Type ls and press Enter.
steps.explain: ls is the command you will type most often. Folders and files are listed by name.

lessons.title: Moving around
lessons.story: Someone left a garden in your home folder, and something is hidden in it. Folders are called directories, and cd (change directory) moves you between them.

files.~/garden/.seed-packet: The hidden seed is a sunflower.

steps.task: Go into the garden directory: cd garden
hints: From your home folder, type cd garden. Watch the prompt change to ~/garden.
steps.explain: The prompt always shows where you are. cd with no arguments takes you back home.

steps.task: Some files are hidden. Show everything with ls -a
hints: Names starting with a dot are hidden from plain ls.
Type ls -a inside the garden.
steps.explain: -a means all. Files whose names start with a dot are hidden by convention, often settings.

steps.task: Read the hidden file with cat to find out what the seed is.
hints: cat prints a file. The file is called .seed-packet (with the dot).
Type cat .seed-packet
steps.explain: cat (from concatenate) prints files. Tab completes names, so cat .se then Tab saves typing.

steps.task: Go back up to your home folder with cd ..
hints: .. means the folder above this one. Type cd ..
steps.explain: .. is the parent folder and . is the current one. They work in every path, like ../garden/shed.

lessons.title: Making, copying and removing
lessons.story: Time to build your own corner of the system: a project folder with a plan in it.

steps.task: Make a directory called projects: mkdir projects
hints: mkdir means make directory. Type mkdir projects in your home folder.
steps.explain: mkdir -p makes a whole path at once, like mkdir -p a/b/c.

steps.task: Write the words learn linux into projects/plan.txt using echo and >
hints: > sends a command's output into a file instead of the screen.
Type echo learn linux > projects/plan.txt
steps.explain: > replaces a file's contents and >> adds to the end. Careful: > overwrites without asking.

steps.task: Make a backup: copy plan.txt to plan.bak in the same folder.
hints: cp takes a source and a destination.
Type cp projects/plan.txt projects/plan.bak
steps.explain: cp copies, mv moves or renames, and both take the source first and the destination second.

steps.task: Open the Files app from the desktop and look inside projects.
hints: Double-click the Files icon on the desktop, then double-click projects.
steps.explain: Files and the terminal show the same filesystem. Change something in one and the other sees it.

steps.task: You don't need the backup after all. Delete projects/plan.bak with rm.
hints: rm removes files. There is no recycle bin in the terminal.
Type rm projects/plan.bak
steps.explain: rm deletes for good. rm -r removes a folder and everything in it, so read twice before pressing Enter.

lessons.title: Reading and searching
lessons.story: A web server has been writing a log all night. Logs are long, so instead of reading everything you'll ask questions about it.

files.~/logs/server.log:
08:00 INFO server started
08:01 INFO request /home
08:02 ERROR database timeout
08:03 INFO request /about
08:04 WARN slow response
08:05 ERROR disk almost full
08:06 INFO request /home
08:07 ERROR database timeout
08:08 INFO request /contact
08:09 INFO server healthy

steps.task: Show only the first 3 lines of logs/server.log with head.
hints: head shows the start of a file. -n chooses how many lines.
Type head -n 3 logs/server.log
steps.explain: tail shows the end instead, which is where the newest log lines are.

steps.task: How many lines does the log have? Count them with wc -l
hints: wc counts lines, words and characters; -l means just lines.
Type wc -l logs/server.log
steps.explain: 10 lines. On a real server, logs can have millions, which is why these tools matter.

steps.task: Show only the ERROR lines with grep.
hints: grep prints the lines that contain a pattern.
Type grep ERROR logs/server.log
steps.explain: grep is one of the most useful commands there is. grep -i ignores case and grep -r searches folders.

steps.task: Now just count the errors with grep -c
hints: -c makes grep print how many lines matched instead of the lines.
Type grep -c ERROR logs/server.log
steps.explain: Three errors. Small questions with exact answers are how you find problems quickly.

lessons.title: Pipes: chaining commands
lessons.story: The real power of the shell is joining small commands together. A pipe | sends one command's output into the next.

files.~/fruit.txt:
banana
apple
cherry
apple
banana
apple

steps.task: Sort fruit.txt alphabetically.
hints: Type sort fruit.txt
steps.explain: sort puts lines in order. sort -r reverses it and sort -n sorts numbers properly.

steps.task: Count how many of each fruit there are by piping sort into uniq -c
hints: uniq only merges repeated lines that are next to each other, so sort first.
Type sort fruit.txt | uniq -c
steps.explain: sort | uniq -c is a classic: it turns a list into a tally. Add | sort -rn to rank it.

steps.task: Save the sorted fruit into sorted.txt using >
hints: Redirection works after any command, including a pipeline.
Type sort fruit.txt > sorted.txt
steps.explain: Commands, pipes and redirection together are how people automate work on Linux.

lessons.title: Permissions and sudo
lessons.story: Linux decides who may read, change or run every file. You'll meet a file you can't read, borrow root's power, and protect a file of your own.

files.~/diary.txt: Today I learned that ls -l shows permissions.

steps.task: See the permissions of your files with ls -l
hints: Type ls -l. The first column, like -rw-r--r--, is the permissions.
steps.explain: rw-r--r-- means: you (owner) can read and write, your group and everyone else can only read.

steps.task: Try to read the password file: cat /etc/shadow
hints: Type cat /etc/shadow. It's supposed to fail!
steps.explain: /etc/shadow holds password hashes, so only root, the administrator, may read it.

steps.task: Run the same command as root by putting sudo in front of it.
hints: sudo means do this as the superuser.
Type sudo cat /etc/shadow
steps.explain: sudo is powerful: root can change or delete anything. Use it only when you understand the command.

steps.task: Make your diary private: only you may read or write it. Use chmod 600 diary.txt
hints: 600 means read+write (6) for you, nothing (0) for group, nothing (0) for others.
Type chmod 600 diary.txt, then ls -l to check.
steps.explain: Each digit adds read (4), write (2) and execute (1). 644 is a typical file and 755 a typical program.
